Name: deception_latent_probe
Title: The Model Knows It Is Lying: Linear Probes for Latent Deception
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM outputs a statement it internally represents as false (deception/knowing hallucination), there exists a linear probe over intermediate activations that separates sincere from deceptive generation, and this probe generalizes across topics and elicitation methods better than output-based lie detection.
Related Work: Azaria & Mitchell (2023) internal states know truthfulness; Burns et al. (2023) discovering latent knowledge (CCS); Marks & Tegmark (2023) geometry of truth; Pacchiardi et al. (2023) lie detection from black-box behavior. Prior probes target truth *representation* of factual statements. We distinguish by targeting *deceptive generation*—cases where the model's belief and its assertion diverge—using role-conditioned lying tasks, and by testing cross-context generalization and robustness to models trained to evade probes.
Abstract: A model that internally represents a claim as false while asserting it as true is deceiving—a critical safety concern for agentic and high-stakes deployments. We hypothesize that deceptive generation leaves a linearly decodable signature in intermediate activations, distinct from mere factual-truth representation, and that a probe trained on this signature generalizes across topics and elicitation methods. We construct paired data where the same model is prompted to answer sincerely versus to lie (via system-prompt role conditioning and incentivized deception games), extract activations at the point of assertion, and train linear probes to distinguish sincere from deceptive states. We evaluate cross-generalization: train on one domain/elicitation, test on others; and stress-test against a model lightly fine-tuned to fool the probe. We compare with black-box lie detectors and with truth-direction probes to establish that we capture belief-assertion divergence rather than topic truth. Metrics: probe AUROC in-distribution and OOD, calibration, and robustness under adaptive pressure. We anticipate probes that generalize moderately across topics but degrade under adaptive evasion, delineating the reliability envelope of activation-based deception detection. This clarifies whether interpretability can provide a trustworthy internal lie detector and under what threat model it holds, an essential input to oversight of increasingly capable systems.
Experiments: 1) Build deception dataset: role-conditioned lying prompts + incentivized deception games (e.g., 'insider trading' scenario from Scheurer et al.), with ground-truth sincere/deceptive labels and known model belief. 2) Extract residual activations at assertion tokens across layers. 3) Train logistic-regression probes; sweep layers. 4) Cross-context eval: train domain A, test domains B,C; train elicitation X, test Y. 5) Adaptive evasion: fine-tune model to minimize probe accuracy while maintaining task reward; re-evaluate. 6) Baselines: Pacchiardi black-box detector, CCS/truth-direction probe. Models: Llama-3-8B/70B-Instruct.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Establishing ground-truth model 'belief' is hard; role-play may not equal genuine deception. Probes can latch onto spurious prompt features. Adaptive evasion may fully defeat probes, bounding usefulness. Results may not transfer to naturally emergent (untrained) deception. Ethical care needed in constructing deception scenarios.
